proves: one gradient reaches the shader by four different paths - a box's background, a path's fill, a path's stroke and a mask - and each draws the ramp rather than a flat colour
checkable: 328x128 on white, eight 72x48 cells at x=8, 88, 168 and 248, the gradient row at y=8..55 and its control row at y=64..111. The ramp runs left to right through #f03c3c, #fad23c, #285ad2. Read each cell against the one BELOW it: the two must differ in colour and not in shape. Ink counts are identical per column - 3456 background, 1140 path fill, 1330 path stroke, 3456 mask - while the pixels differing between the rows are 3456, 1138, 1329 and 3456. Same pixels covered, different colours in them.
checkable_the_ramp_is_a_ramp: a role that took the gradient's first stop and painted it flat would pass a difference test against a flat yellow control. So each cell is read across as well: the background at y=32 reads 242,87,60 at x+6, 247,208,62 at x+36 and 78,112,183 at x+65. The stroke, which is the narrowest ink here, reads 241,70,60 on its left limb at y+44 and 107,128,162 on its right - the same ramp sampled where the shape happens to be.
why_four_roles: three of the four are code paths no other fixture draws. A gradient as a background is in `gradients`; as a path fill, a path stroke and a mask it existed only in a control pair, which says the picture changed and not what it changed into. Both defects that got past every gate this week - the border wedge and the diagonal bottom edge - lived in a branch nothing drew.
why_the_cells_are_not_square: the ramp runs along the long axis of a 72x48 cell, so a direction read off the wrong axis is a different picture rather than a rotated one. A square cell with a diagonal ramp is the arrangement that hides an axis swap.
why_a_triangle_and_not_a_rectangle: a rectangular path filled with a gradient and a box painted with one would be the same picture, and the point of those two cells is that they are different code. The triangle also gives the stroke cell limbs at three angles, so a stroke shader that only worked along one axis would show.
the_mask_control: a mask has no flat equivalent, so its control is the same box unmasked. What the pair says is that the mask removed the right pixels, which is a different claim from the other three - those say a colour arrived.
status: measured from the committed image. Gradient GEOMETRY is Chrome-answerable and worth asking for; the exact interpolated pixels are Skia's arithmetic and are deliberately not pinned to a number - the ramp is read at three points for direction rather than compared ramp against ramp.
